lesson.title: The Frequency Where Reactances Cancel: Finding Resonance
lesson.summary: Resonant frequency is the specific frequency at which an inductor's rising reactance and a capacitor's falling reactance become exactly equal, producing dramatic, frequency selective behavior in LC circuits.
lesson.body:
You have now seen that capacitive reactance Xc = 1/(omega C) falls as frequency rises, while inductive reactance XL = omega L climbs as frequency rises. Since one is falling and the other is rising, as frequency sweeps upward these two curves must cross at exactly one point, a single frequency where Xc and XL happen to be numerically equal. That crossing point is called the resonant frequency, and it marks a genuinely special condition in any circuit containing both an inductor and a capacitor, because the two reactances, equal in magnitude but opposite in their effect on phase, cancel each other out entirely at that frequency, leaving the circuit's behavior dominated by whatever resistance remains.

Setting Xc equal to XL and solving for angular frequency gives the resonant angular frequency directly: 1/(omega0 C) = omega0 L, which rearranges to omega0 squared = 1/(LC), so omega0 = 1 divided by the square root of (LC). Converting to ordinary frequency using omega0 = 2 pi f0 gives the more commonly quoted formula f0 = 1 divided by (2 pi times the square root of LC). This resonant frequency is closely related to the natural frequency of the same L and C combination, since in an ideal lossless LC circuit with no resistance at all, a circuit disturbed and left alone would naturally oscillate back and forth at this exact same frequency on its own, which is why driven resonance and natural free oscillation arrive at the identical formula.

Worked example: reuse the same 100 millihenry inductor and 10 microfarad capacitor from the two previous chapters, so L = 0.1 H and C = 10 times 10 to the minus 6 farads. First compute the product: LC = 0.1 times 0.00001 = 0.000001, or 1 times 10 to the minus 6. Taking the square root: the square root of (1 times 10 to the minus 6) equals 1 times 10 to the minus 3, or 0.001. The resonant angular frequency is omega0 = 1 divided by 0.001 = 1000 rad/s, and converting to hertz, f0 = 1000 divided by 6.2832, approximately 159.15 Hz. Now check that the two reactances really are equal at this frequency: Xc = 1 divided by (1000 times 0.00001) = 1 divided by 0.01 = 100 ohms, and XL = 1000 times 0.1 = 100 ohms. Both come out to exactly 100 ohms, confirming that 159.15 Hz is indeed the resonant frequency for this particular L and C pair.

This cancellation has dramatic practical consequences. In a series RLC circuit, since Xc and XL cancel at resonance, the circuit's total opposition to current drops to just its resistance R, its lowest possible value, causing current to peak sharply at the resonant frequency, exactly the behavior that lets a radio tuner select one station's frequency while rejecting others nearby. In a parallel RLC circuit, the same cancellation instead drives the impedance to its maximum, causing current from the source to drop to a minimum, the opposite effect but stemming from the identical underlying condition, Xc equal to XL.

It is worth noting that below the resonant frequency, XL is smaller than Xc, so the circuit behaves more capacitively overall, while above resonance, XL exceeds Xc, so the circuit behaves more inductively. Resonant frequency, then, is not just a single interesting number, it is the dividing line between two entirely different regimes of circuit behavior, which is exactly why it plays such a central role in designing filters, oscillators, and tuned radio circuits.
